translations: In the distance, Nezha was standing on a shallow beach, holding a dragon tendon, gazing at the sun sinking in the east, his first time without a smile. Clouds were still scattered, and suddenly a wild hemp plant poking out from the brick joints of the Chen Tang Guan city wall wilted halfway. Li Jing was in the courtyard, marking the time, the target was askew, and the bowstring was taut, making a creaking sound. A guard soldier tripped in, scraping off three blocks of wall skin with his boot soles: "Report - a dragon is flying over the East Sea... its tail knocked down seven willow trees!"

No sooner had the words fallen than a golden figure had pinned itself to the courtyard above. Ao Guang hadn't changed into human form, his dragon head hung low, his whiskers like spears, and each scale was dripping with dark, molten lava-like light. He opened his mouth, and the sound wave overturned the clothesline with a row of coarse cloth shirts: "Li Jing! Hand over the demon!"

Li Jing suddenly flung open his sleeve, making a sharp, crisp sound, startling dozens of birds into flight. He took big strides forward, his armor clanking, his finger pointing straight at Nezha's forehead: "Kneel down!"

Nezha stiffened his neck, not moving, his fingernails digging into his palm. Lady Yin suddenly pushed her way out from the crowd, still clutching a half-bundled glutinous rice flour in her hand. She grabbed Nezha's arm and pulled him back, flour scattering down his shoulder: "He's my bone, born after ten months of pregnancy, you want to break him, first break my hands."

Ao Guang's dragon eyes suddenly narrowed, his claw tips crushing the blue tiles under his feet: "You, your son, commits violence, destroys my night demon life, strips my prince's tendons and ligaments - if you don't pay the price today, the East Sea water will flood Chen Tang Guan's three hundred households' stoves!"

The wind was still for a moment. An old man selling tofu quietly placed his pole across the threshold; a barber put down his razor, wiped his sweat, and quietly placed a copper basin on a child's head; several women knelt down, quickly pulling off the red strings from their children's ankles - those were the auspicious threads from last year's Mid-Autumn Festival, now hastily cut off and buried in a clay jar. Nezha glanced at Mrs. Wang next door, who trembled as she brought out a preserved duck she had stored for three years, stuffing it into her neighbor's arms: "Hurry, while they can still walk, take the kids to hide on the high slope."
He moved his throat, finally opening his mouth, his voice hoarse like sandpaper on wood: "It's my fault."

Li Jing's chest was heaving violently, but he didn't say another word. Lady Yin still tightly grasped his wrist, her knuckles white, but that hand slowly relaxed, leaving only a warm imprint. Nezha looked up at Ao Guang's massive shadow looming in the clouds, as everyone held their breath, he slowly raised his right hand, spreading his fingers -

with a piece of dragon tendon lying quietly in the palm of his hand. Ao Guang's throat rolled out a thunderous roar, his whiskers quivering, the East Sea direction suddenly surged with grayish-white waves, pushing forth a stenchy water vapor that hit them face-on. Nezha took a step back, his pants leg scraping against the threshold, pulling off a button. Aman chased after a few steps, a bamboo slip tucked under his arm, writing "Sea Water Enters the City" as he ran, accidentally writing "Enter" like "Chase". Old Zhao glanced over: "This water is indeed chasing us!" Aman hastily corrected it, still stubborn: "It's chasing itself, my brush can't get flustered." Just as he finished speaking, he stepped into a shallow pit, water splashing up to his chin. He first held the green bamboo slip above his head, then swayed in the water, finally steadying himself; when he looked up, Nezha had already leaped onto the city wall, standing firm against the dragon's shadow in the sky.

The city wall began to rise with water. First, the well edge was flooded, then the rice shop's stairs were submerged, and finally, even the stone lion's foot at the Earth God Temple was no longer visible. Children huddled under the eaves, beating the drums wildly. Nezha untied the heavenly net, throwing it fiercely onto the water's surface, the red cloth slicing through the mist, but the next wave still piled on top of the previous one. Aman crouched on the city wall, measuring the water level, ducking his head as the wave came, then peeking out as it receded. Old Zhao asked him if he could see, and he wiped his face, saying: "I can see, the sea is growing faster than my courage." He then quickly added a stroke: Nezha alone tried to block the water, but couldn't.

Nezha refused to admit defeat, spreading the heavenly net across the street, tying each end to stone pillars, trying to block the waves. The first wave hit, the red cloth stretched taut, and the crowd was about to cheer, but the second wave came from the sides, slipping through the doorways, pushing a wooden tub, a gourd dipper, and an empty shoe through the streets. Old Zhao chased after his tofu tub, taking several steps, but couldn't catch up, so he shouted to it: "If you want to go to the East Sea, leave tomorrow's tofu money behind!"

Nezha pulled back a segment of the heavenly net to rescue the tub, but this let the wave from the left side flood over another level of stairs. He finally realized that the sea water wasn't a stationary opponent to be beaten. It would go around the doors, slip through the alleys, and seep through the cracks in the walls; he blocked one place, but another would cry out for help. Several residents brought wooden boards and sandbags to try to build another barrier in the narrow street. Nezha bent down to help, just as he was pressing down the heaviest sandbag, the wooden boards behind it were pushed askew, and with a loud crack, he hit Aman's face with a wave.
